objective: By the end of this lesson you can set and hold best glide within ±10 knots, choose a landing area and fly a planned path to it, run the restart and forced landing checklists, and explain the glide, wind, weather, ELT and ATC knowledge behind every choice.
why: An engine failure gives you one approach with no power to fix mistakes. Pilots who stay composed and know the procedures do best, and the success of an emergency landing is as much a matter of the mind as of skill [[24:350|AFH 18-1]]. At the commercial level the examiner expects that judgment to be sharp and systematic [[1:33|PHAK 1-18]].

prereading.what: Types of emergency landings, psychological hazards, crash safety concepts, terrain selection and types, configuration, the impossible turn.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 18, 18-1 to 18-8

prereading.what: Simulated emergency landings: glide entry, spirals to the key position, restart checks and the sample emergency checklist.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 9, 9-28 to 9-29

prereading.what: Glide ratio, best glide and minimum sink speeds, weight, drag and wind effects, gliding turns and common errors.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 3, 3-21 to 3-24

prereading.what: The lift-to-drag ratio and why total drag is lowest at L/DMAX.
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 5, 5-5 to 5-6

prereading.what: How density altitude, weight, wind and excess speed change landing distance.
prereading.label: PHAK 11-17

prereading.what: Pilot authority, asking for help early, radar help, code 7700, ELTs and search and rescue.
prereading.label: AIM 6-1-1 to 6-2-6

prereading.what: MAYDAY and PAN-PAN calls, emergency frequencies, the distress message and what to do when a crash landing is imminent.
prereading.label: AIM 6-3-1 to 6-3-2

warmup: Think first: your engine quits at 2,500 feet AGL over farmland on a hot, gusty afternoon. Below you are a wheat field beside a road, a plowed field a little farther away, and a shallow river. Which would you choose, what would you do with the airspeed, and in what order would you fly, troubleshoot and talk? Write your answer down and compare it at the end.

key_terms.def: An immediate landing, on or off an airport, because flight cannot continue, for example after an engine failure [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].
A planned landing, on or off an airport, when flight is still possible but unwise, such as for worsening weather, low fuel or developing engine trouble [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].
A forced or precautionary landing on water [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].
The highest lift-to-drag ratio. Flying there gives the least total drag [[1:102|PHAK 5-5]].
The speed that gives the most forward distance for the altitude lost in still air; it occurs at L/DMAX [[24:83|AFH 3-22]].
A speed a few knots below best glide that keeps you in the air longest but covers less distance; not often published [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
Distance traveled compared with altitude lost; 10,000 feet forward for 1,000 feet down is 10 to 1 [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].
Wings, landing gear and fuselage bottom, used to absorb the stop so the cabin stays intact [[24:351|AFH 18-2]].
The point at normal pattern altitude for the chosen field from which you fly a normal power-off approach [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].
Distress (MAYDAY) has absolute priority; urgency (PAN-PAN) has priority over everything except distress [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].
Emergency locator transmitter. Analog units use 121.5 and 243.0 MHz; digital units use 406 MHz and are detected by satellite [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]].
A turn back to the runway after a low-altitude engine failure on takeoff; it needs analysis, a steeper bank and training [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

chunks.title: Three kinds of emergency landing, and the mind game

body.p: The AFH sorts emergency landings into three types [[24:350|AFH 18-1]]. This Task is the forced landing: no power and one approach.

head: Type
What it is
Typical cause
rows: Forced landing
Immediate landing, on or off an airport; flight cannot continue [[24:350|AFH 18-1]]
Engine failure
Precautionary landing
Planned landing, on or off an airport; flight is possible but unwise [[24:350|AFH 18-1]]
Worsening weather, being lost, fuel shortage, engine trouble that is getting worse
Ditching
A forced or precautionary landing on water [[24:350|AFH 18-1]]
Either of the above, over water

body.p: A precautionary landing is usually less hazardous. You have more time to pick terrain and plan, and power to fix errors. Too many precautionary situations turn into forced landings because the pilot used wishful thinking instead of reason [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

bullets: Reluctance to accept the emergency: the mind freezes and you fail to lower the nose, delay picking a field, and hesitate [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].
Undue concern about getting hurt: fear is normal, panic is not. Survival records favor pilots who stay composed [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].
Desire to save the airplane: leads to turning back with too little altitude, stretching the glide, and accepting an approach with no margin [[24:351|AFH 18-2]].

callout.text: Sacrifice the airplane, save the people. Sometimes the goal is simply that everyone walks away [[24:351|AFH 18-2]].

The private and commercial ACS list the same elements for this Task, including best glide ±10 knots (ACS CA.IX.B.S1, PA.IX.B.S1). Commercial training aims at a better understanding of systems and a higher standard of airmanship [[1:33|PHAK 1-18]], so expect deeper questions and a cleaner, more confident flight.

check.q: Why is a precautionary landing generally less hazardous than a forced landing?
check.a: You have more time to pick terrain and plan, and you can use power to fix errors [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

chunks.title: Best glide speed: flying at L/DMAX

body.p: The lift-to-drag ratio (L/D) compares the lift a wing makes with its drag; a higher L/D means a more efficient wing. At L/DMAX total drag is at a minimum, and any angle of attack above or below it raises total drag [[1:102|PHAK 5-5]].
In the figure, induced drag falls as speed rises and parasite drag climbs. The bottom of the total drag curve marks L/DMAX [[1:103|PHAK 5-6]].

Best glide speed is the speed with the greatest forward distance for a given loss of altitude in still air. It occurs at the highest L/D. Glide faster or slower and drag rises, so the glide ratio gets worse [[24:83|AFH 3-22]]. The glide ratio is distance forward compared with height lost [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].

bullets: Weight: does not change the glide angle or the distance if you fly the proper speed. A heavier airplane must glide faster and gets there sooner [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
Drag items: flaps, landing gear and cowl flaps force a lower nose to hold speed, so the glide gets steeper and shorter. Remove them if possible for maximum distance [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
Stretching: back pressure below best glide lands you short and can stall you. Pitch is used only to hold maximum L/D [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

callout.text: ACS: establish and maintain the recommended best glide airspeed, ±10 knots (ACS CA.IX.B.S1). Recommended means your POH/AFM number; the manufacturer's procedures take precedence over the AFH's generic guidance [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

body.p: Precision matters. The AFH says the benefits of best glide come only if you hold it precisely, trimmed, with attitude, sound and feel as your cues [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

callout.text: Propeller overspeed is a special case. The PHAK describes an FAA bulletin where a prop stuck at its low pitch stop, and a speed below published best glide would have given enough thrust for level flight. Follow the POH procedure; look for a better speed only at a safe altitude with time to spare [[1:167|PHAK 7-7]].

check.q: Why does flying 15 knots slower than best glide shorten the glide even though you are "holding the nose up"?
check.a: You are off L/DMAX, so total drag rises and the glide ratio drops [[1:102|PHAK 5-5]] [[24:83|AFH 3-22]].

chunks.title: Minimum sink, wind, and touchdown energy

head: Best glide
Minimum sink
rows: Goal
Most distance for the altitude lost [[24:83|AFH 3-22]]
Most time in the air, lowest rate of sink [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]
Speed
At L/DMAX [[24:83|AFH 3-22]]
Lower; generally a few knots below best glide [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]
Distance
Greatest in still air
Less distance traveled [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]
In the POH?
Normally published
Not often published [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]
When to use
Reaching a field
When time aloft matters more than distance, such as ditching at sea [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]

body.p: Wind changes glide distance over the ground. A tailwind carries you farther because of the higher groundspeed; a headwind shortens the glide [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. You cannot control the wind, only correct for it [[24:174|AFH 9-3]].

The wind also sets how hard you hit. Groundspeed is the most critical factor in crash severity: doubling the groundspeed quadruples the destructive energy. Even a small change in touchdown groundspeed, from wind or technique, changes the outcome. Touch down at the lowest controllable airspeed with all aerodynamic devices [[24:352|AFH 18-3]].

Application: a tailwind can help you reach an area, but plan the final approach into the wind when you can. The AFH night list also says to stay oriented to the wind to avoid a downwind landing [[24:230|AFH 11-13]].
On final into a strong headwind, the AFH lists flying slightly above best glide to stabilize the rest of the approach [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].

callout.text: Twice the groundspeed, four times the energy [[24:352|AFH 18-3]].

check.q: When would minimum sink speed be the better choice than best glide?
check.a: When time in the air matters more than distance, such as when ditching at sea [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

chunks.title: Atmosphere: density altitude, carb ice, snow, water and night

body.p: Thin air needs more true airspeed (TAS) for the same angle of attack. Warm, humid air is less dense, so a hot humid day needs more TAS too [[1:102|PHAK 5-5]].

bullets: Density altitude: you land at the same indicated airspeed but a higher TAS. Minimum landing distance at 5,000 feet is 16 percent more than at sea level, about 3.5 percent per 1,000 feet [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].
The worst case: high weight, high density altitude and an unfavorable wind together [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].
Application: higher TAS means higher groundspeed at touchdown, and energy grows with the square of groundspeed [[24:352|AFH 18-3]].

Carburetor ice: with the throttle closed the engine cools fast and ices more easily. If icing is suspected, apply full carburetor heat before closing the throttle and open the throttle briefly now and then to keep the engine warm [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]. Carburetor heat is on the restart list [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].
Reading the wind: windsock, smoke, dust, brush fires, wind farms and patterns on water [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].
Water and snow: a smooth wide surface can rob you of depth perception. Drag it in with power if you have it; a snow landing is flown like a ditching [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].
Night: a forced landing may bring terrain hazards you cannot see, and an accessory failure such as the alternator can take the electrical system with it [[30:26|RMH 3-8]].

body.p: The AFH gives a separate list for an engine failure at night [[24:230|AFH 11-13]]. You will put it in order next.

callout.text: Leaving partial carburetor heat on, or too little time, can make icing worse. Full heat stays on until normal power returns [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

check.q: At a high density altitude field, does the airspeed indicator show a higher touchdown speed?
check.a: No. Indicated airspeed is the same, but TAS and groundspeed are higher, so you need more distance [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

chunks.title: Immediate actions, restart attempts and the checklist

body.p: Entry: if you are faster than best glide, let the airplane slow (you may even climb to bleed off speed), then lower the nose and trim. If you are at or below best glide, lower the nose at once. Make sure flaps and gear suit the situation [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

Excess airspeed is a gift: it can be turned into distance or altitude [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]. Hold altitude with back pressure while the speed decays, then set the glide attitude and trim [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
Immediate action items are best committed to memory. Once they are done, and as workload permits, compare what you did with the checklist [[24:284|AFH 13-35]].

head: Critical item
Why it matters
rows: Fuel selector and fuel in the selected tank
Many actual emergency landings came from a selector on an empty tank while the other tank was full. Switch tanks even if the gauges show fuel; gauges can be wrong [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]
Fuel pressure and electric pump
The gauge shows whether the pump is needed [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]; a boost pump can cure vapor-related flow problems [[24:283|AFH 13-34]]
Mixture
Check its position [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]; changing it may help [[24:283|AFH 13-34]]
Magnetos
Check the switch [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]; an engine may run on one magneto [[24:283|AFH 13-34]]
Carburetor heat or alternate air
Ice or a blocked intake [[24:200|AFH 9-29]] [[24:283|AFH 13-34]]

body.p: If the engine runs roughly, use whatever power it gives. It is still generally better to switch the engine and fuel off just before touchdown [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

callout.text: Build the habit of checking the critical restart items while you pick a field and plan the approach. The AFH admits that doing both is hard early in training [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].
Figure 9-29 is a sample. Your POH/AFM procedure comes first whenever it differs from the AFH [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

check.q: The engine quits and both fuel gauges show fuel. Should you still switch tanks?
check.a: Yes. Fuel gauges can be inaccurate, and a selector on an empty tank has caused many actual emergency landings [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

body.p: Your choice of sites depends on three things: the route you picked in preflight planning, your height above the ground, and any excess airspeed [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

callout.text: Except for takeoff and landing, fly at an altitude that allows an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property on the surface if the engine fails [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(a)]]. Route and altitude planning is your first forced landing decision.

body.p: Only the low, slow part of the takeoff leaves you a very limited choice, and even then a few degrees of heading change may make a crash survivable [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

High up, choose the general area first and the exact spot later; terrain can look very different from altitude. Drop your plan for one that is obviously better, but as a rule change your mind only once. A well-flown crash landing in poor terrain can be less hazardous than an uncontrolled touchdown on a good field [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].
With a big choice of fields up high, inexperienced pilots tend to delay the decision, and errors in maneuvering and glide estimates creep in [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

Plan the approach around wind, field size and slope, and obstacles on final. They rarely agree. Aim for the mix that leaves a margin for error. It is sometimes better to approach over open ground regardless of wind, because hitting something at the end of the slide is far less hazardous than hitting it at flying speed before touchdown [[24:353|AFH 18-4]] [[24:354|AFH 18-5]].

head: Terrain
What the AFH says
rows: Dense mature crops (corn, grain)
Almost as good as a runway arresting device; damage can be repairable [[24:351|AFH 18-2]]
Brush and small trees
Real cushioning and braking without destroying the airplane [[24:351|AFH 18-2]]
Open spot ringed by trees
Avoid it if the ground can be reached only by a steep descent [[24:354|AFH 18-5]]
River or creek
Make sure you can reach the water or creek bed without snagging the wings [[24:354|AFH 18-5]]
Road
Obstacles beside it may stay hidden until late; wires usually run alongside, so look for the poles [[24:354|AFH 18-5]]

check.q: Your engine fails at 7,000 feet AGL. Do you pick a spot right away?
check.a: No. Pick the general area first, then the spot as you get lower, because terrain from altitude can mislead [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

chunks.title: Surviving the touchdown: structure, attitude and terrain

body.p: Avoiding crash injuries comes down to two things: keep the cabin intact by letting dispensable structure (wings, gear, belly) absorb the stop, and keep bodies from hitting the inside of the cabin through seat and harness security [[24:351|AFH 18-2]].

Little stopping distance is needed if the deceleration is spread evenly. A typical light airplane is designed to protect occupants at 9 G forward. At a uniform 9 G it stops in about 9.4 feet from 50 mph, and about 37.6 feet from 100 mph [[24:352|AFH 18-3]].

Keep control of attitude and sink rate at touchdown; losing it is the most critical error. A nose-low attitude can stick the nose in, and a steep bank near the ground raises stall speed and risks a wingtip strike. A flat touchdown well over 500 fpm on a hard surface can injure occupants even when the cabin holds, especially in a low-wing gear-up landing [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

bullets: Trees: normal landing configuration, into the wind, minimum airspeed but not below stall, nose-high so the belly and both wings hit first [[24:355|AFH 18-6]].
Pick low, closely spaced trees with dense crowns. Tall, thin tops allow a long free fall; 75 feet means about 40 knots, or 4,000 fpm [[24:355|AFH 18-6]].
Keep the fuselage off heavy trunks. Steer between two trunks only once on the ground, never while airborne [[24:355|AFH 18-6]].
Confined area: with little room left, forcing the airplane onto the ground can beat waiting for it to settle, since it slows faster on the ground [[24:354|AFH 18-5]].
Water: ditched at minimum speed in a normal attitude, an airplane floats for at least several minutes on its wings and tanks [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

callout.text: Slow, level, belly first, both wings at once [[24:352|AFH 18-3]] [[24:355|AFH 18-6]].

check.q: Why are low trees with wide, dense crowns better than tall trees with thin tops?
check.a: Tall thin tops allow too much free fall; a 75-foot fall means about 40 knots at impact [[24:355|AFH 18-6]].

chunks.title: Flying the path: spirals, the key position and a stabilized glide

body.p: Hold one gliding speed. Changing it ruins your judgment of glide distance and where you will land [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].
Use any mix of straight glides and spirals to arrive at the normal key position, at normal pattern altitude, for your field. From there it is a normal power-off approach [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

Energy view: total energy is altitude (mgh) plus speed (one half mV squared) [[24:87|AFH 4-1]]. The elevator trades one for the other [[24:90|AFH 4-4]]. Application: with the engine dead nothing adds energy, so every turn, slip and flap setting only decides how you spend what you have.

A stabilized approach is a constant-angle path to a chosen point at a constant speed and configuration [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]. The AFH list (path, heading, speed, configuration, sink rate, power, checklists) is a guide; focus on the elements rather than insisting on every one [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. With no engine the power item does not apply.

bullets: Fixes for misjudged height: slips, flaps, moving the base leg, and changing the turn onto final [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].
Forward slip: starts a descent faster than flaps and can be taken out with no penalty; retracting flaps can cost altitude [[24:185|AFH 9-14]].
Flaps: lower stall speed and help at slow speed, but early flaps throw away altitude and can ruin a sound plan [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

Complete power failure: keep best glide until you configure for landing and plan a steeper approach than usual. Start slowing the descent at about 10 percent of your sink rate (100 feet at 1,000 fpm) [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

callout.text: You cannot dive at a field and land on it. Too much speed is as dangerous as too little: you float and overshoot [[24:199|AFH 9-28]] [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]. A sink rate over 800 to 1,000 fpm on final is excessive [[24:201|AFH 9-30]].

body.p: Changing the plan (R2): normally fly the field you chose. Switch only if it would obviously end in disaster and a better field is within gliding distance, and know the hazards of hard maneuvering down low [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

check.q: You arrive at the key position 400 feet high. Name two AFH tools to fix it.
check.a: Any two of: a forward slip, earlier flaps, a wider base leg, or a changed turn onto final [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

chunks.title: Configuration, securing the airplane and touchdown

body.p: Flaps on final are recommended when time allows, because they lower stall speed and improve slow-speed handling. Time them carefully [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

Retractable gear has no hard and fast rule. In rugged terrain, trees, or a high sink rate impact, extended gear protects the cabin, but a collapsing gear can rupture a fuel tank. When a normal touchdown is assured with ample room, a gear-up landing on level soft ground or across a plowed field may cause less damage. The AFM/POH recommendation wins [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

Turning off the electrical system before touchdown lowers the chance of a post-crash fire, but leave the master on until you no longer need electrical power for vital systems, such as electric flaps [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

callout.text: Positive control of the airplane on final has priority over everything else, including configuration and checklist items [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

body.p: The sample forced landing checklist ends: airspeed, mixture idle cutoff, fuel selector off, ignition off, flaps as required, master off, doors unlatched before touchdown, touchdown slightly tail low, brakes heavily [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

On the checkride (S5, S6): the evaluator will not simulate a power failure in a single-engine airplane unless a safe landing is possible (ACS Appendix 2). Simulated steps may differ from a real emergency, and each step is called out [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]. Keep the engine warm and cleared, and be clear who has the throttle [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]. The approach ends as soon as it is clear whether a safe landing was assured, never creating a hazard to people or property [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

callout.text: Application: in a simulated emergency, touch and call the shutdown items (mixture, fuel, ignition, master) rather than moving them, unless the examiner briefs otherwise. When you recover, add power as the 10 percent lead appears [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

check.q: You have electric flaps and the field made. When does the master switch go off?
check.a: After you no longer need electrical power, so after the flaps are set [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

chunks.title: Calling for help: ATC, 7700, 121.5 and ELTs

body.p: You are in at least an urgency condition the moment you doubt your position, fuel, weather or anything else that affects safety. That is the time to ask for help [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. In an emergency needing immediate action the PIC may deviate from part 91 rules as needed, and must send a written report if the FAA asks [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3]].

head: Tool
How to use it
rows: Frequency

The one in use first. Otherwise 121.5 MHz, guarded by direction finding stations, military towers, most civil towers and radar facilities. If an ARTCC does not answer on 121.5, call the nearest tower [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]]
Words
MAYDAY, preferably three times, for distress; it has absolute priority and commands radio silence. PAN-PAN for urgency [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]]
Transponder

Keep your assigned code while in radio contact unless told otherwise; if you cannot reach ATC right away, squawk 7700 with Mode C [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]. Code 7700 normally sets off an alarm at every control position [[34:29|AIM 6-2-2]]
Message

As many as needed, in order: MAYDAY, station, aircraft ID and type, nature of distress, weather, intentions, position and heading, altitude, fuel in minutes, people on board, anything useful [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]
Crash landing imminent
Add ELT status, landmarks, airplane color, people on board and emergency gear; turn on the ELT if you can; set the radio to continuous transmit if fire risk is not a concern [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]
After landing
Stay with the airplane unless you have good reason to think you will not be found [[34:47|AIM 6-3-2]]

body.p: Radar help to a VFR pilot is advice; you remain responsible for flying the airplane safely [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]].

ELTs: analog units transmit on 121.5 and 243.0 MHz; 406 MHz units are digital, must be registered with NOAA, and can be decoded by the Cospas-Sarsat satellites. Satellite monitoring of 121.5 and 243.0 stopped on February 1, 2009, so a 121.5-only ELT depends on a nearby facility or an overflying aircraft hearing it. SAR can respond to a 406 alert in minutes, against possibly hours for 121.5. An activated ELT transmits for at least 48 hours, and you should know how to turn it on by hand [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]] [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

14 CFR 91.207 requires an approved ELT (personal or automatic type for most part 91 flying). Replace or recharge the battery after 1 cumulative hour of use or when 50 percent of its useful life is gone [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207]]. Inspect the ELT within 12 calendar months. Training flights entirely within 50 NM of the departure airport are exempt [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)-(f)]].

Testing: analog ELTs only in the first 5 minutes after the hour, no more than three sweeps; airborne tests are not authorized. Listen on 121.5 before engine shutdown to catch a false activation [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

Search and rescue: a filed flight plan is the most timely sign that you are overdue. An injured survivor's life expectancy can drop as much as 80 percent in the first 24 hours, and without a flight plan about 36 hours normally pass before anyone raises the alarm [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].

callout.text: A real off-airport landing with serious injury or substantial damage is an aircraft accident under NTSB rules [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]]; the reporting duties are in Task CA.III.A.

check.q: Your MAYDAY to the ARTCC on 121.5 gets no answer. What does the AIM say to do?

chunks.title: The impossible turn, as the AFH teaches it

body.p: If the engine fails in the initial climb, lower the nose and set the glide attitude. Going straight ahead or turning slightly gives you time to set up and land under control as slowly as possible; it is usually the lowest-risk choice [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

Turning back needs analysis. Do it only if you are certain the airplane can reach the field and you have trained the maneuver. Risks: a wingtip strike and cartwheel, an accelerated stall if the nose is not lowered, and a downwind landing at high groundspeed [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

The FAA example: engine failure at 300 feet AGL, 4 seconds to react, then a standard-rate turn (3° per second) at 65 knots. The 180° takes a minute and leaves you 4,200 feet to the side, so you need 225° in all: 75 seconds plus 4. At about 1,000 fpm you lose about 1,316 feet and end up 1,016 feet below the runway [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

bullets: A turn back, if attempted, needs a steeper bank; a standard-rate turn takes too long and too much room [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].
Know the altitude loss for your make and model and whether it can glide back. Practice both directions at a safe altitude, and expect the high end of your range in a real event [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].
The better direction is usually into the crosswind. Do not attempt a turn back unless it will succeed [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].
It is an unacceptable risk for students, low-time or untrained pilots, and airplanes with too little glide performance [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

body.p: Gliding steep turns near the ground are dangerous: too much rudder into the bank while pulling back can become an unrecoverable spin [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

callout.text: Brief it before takeoff: the AFH says to consider your options and the preferred direction for emergency turns from the departure path, altitude, wind and terrain [[24:133|AFH 6-1]]. A cruise climb pitch, lower than VY, gives you more time to react to a power failure [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

check.q: Why does the AFH example with a standard-rate turn end 1,016 feet below the runway?
check.a: A standard-rate turn takes too long: 225° plus reaction is 79 seconds, and at 1,000 fpm that costs about 1,316 feet from 300 feet AGL [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

chunks.title: Risk: traffic, low-altitude handling and distraction

bullets: Collision hazards: clear the airspace in the direction of turns and descent; failing to do so is a listed glide error [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. Spirals over a field keep your eyes on the field, so keep scanning. Wires along roads may show only by their poles [[24:354|AFH 18-5]].
Announce: at night the AFH says to report to ATC or UNICOM and not to change frequency unless told to [[24:230|AFH 11-13]].

Low altitude: avoid cross-controlled gliding turns near the ground [[24:85|AFH 3-24]], steep banks just before touchdown [[24:353|AFH 18-4]], and stretching the glide over obstacles [[24:354|AFH 18-5]].
CFIT and loss of control: poor energy management is a factor in loss of control, CFIT and approach-and-landing accidents, the three most common fatal accident types [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].
Distraction: airplanes have been lost through fixation on the engine problem while nobody flew the airplane [[24:283|AFH 13-34]].
Examiners add realistic distractions, and failing to use sound ADM in a Task fails that Task (ACS Appendix 2).

callout.text: Fly first. Positive control comes before configuration and checklists [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].
Confusion over who has the throttle has caused many near accidents in simulated emergency landings. Settle it before the maneuver [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

check.q: What does the AFH say happens when a pilot fixates on the engine problem?
check.a: Airplanes have been lost because the pilot stopped flying the airplane [[24:283|AFH 13-34]].

chunks.title: Fly it on the checkride, step by step

body.p: Brief first: your POH best glide speed, flap and gear advice, the restart and forced landing checklists, who has the throttle, and how the examiner wants it to end [[24:200|AFH 9-29]] (ACS CA.IX.B.S5).

bullets: 1. The examiner closes the throttle and calls a simulated emergency landing [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].
2. Fast: hold altitude or climb until best glide, then lower the nose and trim. Slow: lower the nose now. Hold best glide ±10 knots [[24:199|AFH 9-28]] (ACS CA.IX.B.S1).
3. Clean up drag (flaps, gear, cowl flaps) per the POH for the most glide [[24:84|AFH 3-23]] (ACS CA.IX.B.S2).
4. Pick a field within reach, read the wind, and point the field out to the examiner [[24:199|AFH 9-28]] (ACS CA.IX.B.S3).
5. Turn toward it and plan straight glides or spirals to the key position at pattern altitude [[24:199|AFH 9-28]] (ACS CA.IX.B.S4).
6. Touch and call the restart items: fuel selector, mixture, carburetor heat, magnetos, primer [[24:200|AFH 9-29]] (ACS CA.IX.B.S6).
7. Simulate the radio call and 7700; say what you would transmit without transmitting it [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].
8. From the key position, fly a normal power-off approach; fix height with slips, flaps, base placement and the turn to final [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].
9. Touch and call the forced landing items in order, flaps before the master [[24:200|AFH 9-29]] [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].
10. End it as briefed: a go-around or a landing, starting the recovery at the 10 percent lead [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

callout.text: Call your field and your plan out loud. The examiner grades your judgment, and you cannot get credit for thinking you did not share (application).

check.q: The examiner closes the throttle while you are 20 knots faster than best glide. What do you do first?
check.a: Hold altitude (or climb) until the speed bleeds to best glide, then lower the nose and trim [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

head: Error
Fix
rows: Lowering the nose before the speed decays to glide speed [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Hold altitude with back pressure, then pitch and trim [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]
Chasing the airspeed indicator or flying the glide by instruments alone [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Hold the attitude, trim, and use sound and feel [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]
Delaying the field choice while high [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]
Choose the area early, then the spot [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]
Diving at the field and arriving too fast [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]
One constant glide speed all the way [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]
Flaps too early, losing a sound plan [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]
Add flaps when the field is made
Stretching the glide with back pressure [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Keep best glide; land short under control rather than stall [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]
Skids, slips or cross-control in gliding turns near the ground [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Coordinated turns, constant bank, less rudder than with power [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Forgetting the critical restart items [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]
Run them while you plan, by memory, then the checklist [[24:284|AFH 13-35]]
Changing fields late or more than once [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]
Switch only for an obviously better field within reach [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]

callout.text: Eagerness to get down is one of the most common faults in simulated emergency landings [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

check.q: Which glide error leads to an overly steep glide right after the throttle is closed?
check.a: Too little back pressure during glide entry [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

f1.caption: Figure 5-6. Drag versus speed.
f1.alt: Graph of drag against airspeed: a red induced drag curve falls as speed rises, a green parasite drag curve climbs, and a dotted total drag curve has its lowest point, marked minimum drag, where the two cross.

f2.caption: Figure 9-29. Sample emergency checklist.
f2.alt: Sample POH checklist page: engine failure during flight restart procedures (airspeed 70 KIAS, carburetor heat on, fuel selector both, mixture rich, ignition both or start, primer in and locked) and emergency landing without engine power (airspeed, mixture idle cutoff, fuel selector off, ignition off, flaps as required, master off, doors unlatched, touchdown slightly tail low, brakes heavily).

f3.caption: Figure 9-28. Remain over intended landing area.
f3.alt: An airplane retracts its flaps, then spirals down over a field in descending loops, with a wind arrow at the side; at the base key point it lowers flaps and rolls out on a final toward a striped landing path.

f4.caption: Figure 18-1. Using vegetation to absorb energy.
f4.alt: A high-wing airplane stopped deep in tall green crops, cabin intact, the vegetation having absorbed its energy.

f5.caption: Figure 18-3. Intentional gear-up landing.
f5.alt: View past an airplane wing toward a patchwork of level plowed and crop fields stretching to the horizon.

f6.caption: Figure 18-4. Tree landing.
f6.alt: An airplane resting in the dense crowns of a stand of trees, both wings in the branches, with a loose wheel and a bent landing gear leg lying on the ground among the trunks.

f7.caption: Figure 18-5. Turning back to the runway after engine failure.
f7.alt: An airplane loses its engine at 300 feet AGL after takeoff and turns back; after 180 degrees it is 4,480 feet to the side, and after 225 degrees it is 1,016 feet below runway level.

scenario.title: Repositioning flight: a quiet engine over farm country
scenario.setup: You are repositioning a retractable-gear single for its owner on a hot afternoon (30°C) at 4,500 feet MSL, about 3,500 feet AGL, at cruise speed. You are on VFR flight following with a discrete code. Wind is from the west at 15 knots. The engine runs rough for a few seconds, then quits. Below are rolling farm fields, a two-lane road with poles alongside, and a large plowed field to the west.

questions.q: You are 50 knots faster than best glide. What do you do with that speed?
questions.a: Hold altitude, or climb, while it bleeds off to best glide, then lower the nose and trim [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. Excess airspeed can be turned into altitude or distance [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

questions.q: At 3,500 feet AGL, how do you pick a field?
questions.a: Choose the general area first and refine the spot as you descend, since terrain looks different from altitude. Change your mind only once [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

questions.q: Both fuel gauges read a quarter tank and the selector is on the right tank. What do you do?
questions.a: Switch tanks anyway and run the other critical items: pump and pressure, mixture, magnetos, alternate air or carburetor heat [[24:283|AFH 13-34]]. Gauges can be wrong [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

questions.q: How do you use the radio and transponder?
questions.a: Stay on the approach frequency, keep your assigned code, and transmit MAYDAY three times with the message elements [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]] [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]. Squawk 7700 only if you cannot reach ATC right away [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].

questions.q: How does the 30°C day change your landing?
questions.a: Same indicated speed but higher TAS, so higher groundspeed and a longer landing [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. Energy at impact grows with the square of groundspeed [[24:352|AFH 18-3]], so land into the wind on the plowed field.

questions.q: The touchdown is assured on the long, soft plowed field. Gear up or down, and when do you shut things off?
questions.a: A gear-up landing on level soft or plowed ground may cause less damage when a normal touchdown and ample stopping room are assured, but follow the POH [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]. Switch engine and fuel off just before touchdown and the master once you no longer need electrical power [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]. After landing, stay with the airplane [[34:47|AIM 6-3-2]].

skills.do: Sets the POH best glide speed promptly and holds it within 10 knots either way, trimmed, all the way to the key position.
skills.practice: Practice glide entries from cruise and from climb: bleed to best glide, then pitch and trim [[24:199|AFH 9-28]] [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

skills.do: Configures per the POH and the situation: drag cleaned up for the glide, flaps and gear set for the landing at the right time.
skills.practice: Say each configuration change and why; hold flaps until the field is made [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

skills.do: Picks a suitable field within gliding distance, allowing for altitude, wind, terrain and obstructions, and points it out.
skills.practice: On every cross-country, name the field you would use right now and the wind direction [[24:199|AFH 9-28]] [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

skills.do: Plans and flies a path, straight or spiraling, to the key position and a normal power-off approach to the field.
skills.practice: Spiral down over a chosen field to the key position from different heights [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

skills.do: Prepares for landing exactly as the examiner briefed: landing checklist items called, and a go-around or landing at the agreed point.
skills.practice: Agree on the go-around point and who has the throttle before each practice [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

skills.do: Completes the restart checklist while planning the approach, then the forced landing checklist, using touch and call.
skills.practice: Chair-fly the POH restart and forced landing flows until they are automatic [[24:200|AFH 9-29]] [[24:284|AFH 13-35]].

quiz.q: Which type of emergency landing is a planned landing made while flight is still possible but unwise?
options: Forced landing
Ditching
Precautionary landing
Emergency descent
quiz.why: A precautionary landing is a premeditated landing when further flight is possible but inadvisable [[24:350|AFH 18-1]]. A forced landing is immediate because flight cannot continue.

quiz.q: What is true of total drag when you fly at L/DMAX?
options: It is at its maximum
It is at its minimum
It equals induced drag alone
It changes with weight only
quiz.why: At L/DMAX total drag is at a minimum; higher or lower angles of attack increase it [[1:102|PHAK 5-5]].

quiz.q: For a crash landing in poor terrain, which factor does the AFH call most critical to the severity of the stop?
options: Groundspeed
Flap setting
Fuel on board
Altitude when the engine failed
quiz.why: Severity depends on groundspeed and stopping distance, and speed is the most critical: doubling groundspeed quadruples the destructive energy [[24:352|AFH 18-3]].

quiz.q: You land at a high density altitude field. Compared with a sea-level field, what is the same?
options: True airspeed at touchdown
Groundspeed at touchdown
Indicated airspeed at touchdown
Landing distance
quiz.why: You land at the same IAS, but TAS is higher, so the landing distance is longer [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

quiz.q: Many actual emergency landings were later traced to what?
options: Magneto switches left on BOTH
The fuel selector on an empty tank while another tank had fuel
Carburetor heat used too early
Flaps set to takeoff
quiz.why: The AFH notes many emergency landings came from a selector on an empty tank with plenty of fuel in the other [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

quiz.q: According to the AFH, excess airspeed when the engine fails can be converted into what?
options: Only a longer landing roll
Engine power
Distance and/or altitude
Nothing useful
quiz.why: Excess airspeed is one of the factors governing site choice, because it can be converted into distance or altitude [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

quiz.q: About what impact speed results from a 75-foot free fall out of tall trees?
options: About 10 knots
About 25 knots
About 40 knots
About 75 knots
quiz.why: The AFH says a free fall from 75 feet gives about 40 knots, or about 4,000 fpm [[24:355|AFH 18-6]].

quiz.q: After spiraling down over your field, what do you fly from the key position on?
options: A normal power-off approach
A short-field approach with power
A straight-in at minimum sink
Another full spiral
quiz.why: From the key point on, the approach is a normal power-off approach [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

quiz.q: You call an ARTCC on 121.5 MHz and get no answer. What does the AIM say to do?
options: Switch to 243.0 MHz only
Call the nearest tower
Stop transmitting and wait
Change your code to 7600
quiz.why: ARTCC emergency frequency coverage is limited; if an ARTCC does not respond on 121.5 or 243.0, call the nearest tower [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].

quiz.q: If a turn back to the runway is attempted after a low-altitude engine failure, what does the AFH say it requires?
options: A standard-rate turn to limit load factor
A higher bank angle than standard rate
Full flaps before the turn
A climb to gain altitude first
quiz.why: The FAA example shows a standard-rate or shallow turn takes too much time and distance; a turn back needs a higher bank [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

final_quiz.q: Your engine fails at 6,500 feet AGL over hilly farmland with several fields in view. What is the best first step in choosing where to land?
options: Pick the nearest specific spot and commit to it
Pick the general area first, then the exact spot lower down
Circle until you find a paved road
Head straight for the farthest airport you might reach
final_quiz.why: From considerable height, choose the general area first; terrain looks very different from altitude and much height can be lost pinpointing a spot [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

final_quiz.q: A crash landing is imminent. Beyond the normal distress message, which extra details does the AIM suggest you give?
options: ELT status, visible landmarks and airplane color
Your certificate number and medical class
The last altimeter setting and your squawk history
Your instructor's name and home airport
final_quiz.why: With a crash landing imminent, add ELT status, visible landmarks, aircraft color, persons on board and emergency equipment [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].

final_quiz.q: Your retractable is gliding toward rugged, tree-covered terrain with no open field in reach. What does the AFH say about the gear?
options: Always land gear up to protect the fuel tanks
Extended gear would protect the cabin, weighed against a ruptured tank; follow the POH
Gear position never matters
Lower the gear only if over water
final_quiz.why: In rugged terrain and trees, or at a high sink rate, extended gear protects the cabin, but a collapsing gear may rupture a fuel tank; follow the AFM/POH [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

final_quiz.q: You flare a low-wing airplane with the gear up onto a hard dry lakebed and let it settle flat at about 900 fpm. What does the AFH warn about?
options: Nothing, a flat attitude always protects occupants
A flat touchdown well above 500 fpm on a hard surface can injure occupants even if the cabin holds
The gear will extend on impact
The airplane will float too far
final_quiz.why: A flat touchdown at a high sink rate, well over 500 fpm, on a hard surface can be injurious without destroying the cabin, especially gear up in a low-wing airplane [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

final_quiz.q: A flight school airplane will fly only training flights entirely within 25 NM of its base, and its ELT is out for repair. Does 14 CFR 91.207 ground it?
options: Yes, no flight is allowed without an ELT
No, training operations entirely within 50 NM of the departure airport are excepted
Only if passengers are carried
Only at night
final_quiz.why: 91.207(a) does not apply to aircraft engaged in training operations conducted entirely within a 50-NM radius of the airport where they began [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)-(f)]].

final_quiz.q: Your ELT transmitted for 70 minutes, in total, during an inadvertent activation and a search. What does 91.207 require?
options: Nothing until the annual inspection
Replace or recharge the battery, since it has been in use more than 1 cumulative hour
Remove the ELT permanently
Test it in flight
final_quiz.why: Batteries must be replaced or recharged when the transmitter has been used for more than 1 cumulative hour [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207]]. Airborne tests are not authorized [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

final_quiz.q: You are touching down a little fast in a small field and a stone wall is coming up at the far end. What does the AFH favor?
options: Pull up and try to clear the wall
Get the airplane onto the ground; hitting something at the end of the slide beats hitting it at flying speed
Hold it off as long as possible to bleed speed in the air
Make a steep turn to land beside the wall
final_quiz.why: The airplane slows faster on the ground than in the air, so forcing it down can be better [[24:354|AFH 18-5]], and an obstacle at the end of the ground slide is much less hazardous than one at flying speed [[24:354|AFH 18-5]].

final_quiz.q: Before you consider any turn back after a takeoff engine failure, what must you know according to the AFH?
options: Only the runway length
The expected altitude loss in the turn for your make and model and whether it can glide back
The tower frequency
The standard-rate turn radius at 100 knots
final_quiz.why: A pilot considering a turn back should know the expected altitude loss for the specific make and model and whether it can physically glide back [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

final_quiz.q: When practicing turn backs at altitude, which direction does the AFH say is usually better?
options: Always to the left
Into the crosswind
Away from the crosswind
Toward the downwind side
final_quiz.why: Training should determine the better direction to turn back, usually into a crosswind [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

final_quiz.q: Cruising VFR, you become unsure whether your fuel will last to the destination. According to the AIM, when are you at least in an urgency condition?
options: Only once the engine stops
The moment you become doubtful about fuel endurance
When fuel is below 30 minutes
Only after you declare it
final_quiz.why: An aircraft is in at least an urgency condition the moment the pilot becomes doubtful about position, fuel endurance or weather; ask for help then [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

final_quiz.q: In a simulated emergency on your checkride, when should the approach be ended?
options: Only after touchdown on the field
As soon as it can be determined whether a safe landing is assured, without creating a hazard on the ground
At exactly 1,000 feet AGL
When the examiner falls silent
final_quiz.why: Every simulated emergency landing approach ends once it can be determined whether a safe landing is assured, never continuing to an undue hazard or annoyance to people or property [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

final_quiz.q: Your engine quits over a wide, snow-covered frozen field in flat light. You are in a low-wing retractable. Which plan fits the AFH?
options: Full flaps, gear down, steep approach
Treat it like a ditching: no more than intermediate flaps, gear up unless the POH says otherwise, and watch for whiteout
Land as fast as possible to keep control
Use minimum sink speed all the way to touchdown, no flaps, gear down
final_quiz.why: A snow landing is flown like a ditching, with the same configuration and the same care about lost depth perception: no more than intermediate flaps on low-wing airplanes and retractable gear up unless the AFM/POH advises otherwise [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

final_quiz.q: On final to your forced landing field you are high, with flaps not yet extended. Which AFH point makes a forward slip attractive here?
options: It adds airspeed for the flare
It starts the descent faster than flaps and can be removed with no penalty
It is the only way to lower stall speed
It lets you stretch the glide later
final_quiz.why: In a real engine failure a forward slip starts a descent more quickly than flaps and can be removed without penalty, while retracting flaps can cost altitude [[24:185|AFH 9-14]].

takeaways: Fly first: positive control beats configuration and checklists [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].
Best glide is L/DMAX; hold the POH speed ±10 knots and never stretch it [[1:102|PHAK 5-5]] [[24:84|AFH 3-23]] (ACS CA.IX.B.S1).
Pick the area early, the spot later, and change your mind only once [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].
Run the restart items while you plan; switch tanks even if the gauges show fuel [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].
Arrive at the key position at pattern altitude at a constant glide speed, then fly a normal power-off approach [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].
Touch down at the lowest controllable speed, into the wind if you can; groundspeed is energy [[24:352|AFH 18-3]].
Ask for help early: MAYDAY on the frequency in use, keep your code if in contact, otherwise 7700 [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].
cfi_notes: Figure 18-5 labels the side offset 4,480 feet, while the AFH text says 4,200 feet [[24:356|AFH 18-7]]. Teach the altitude point (1,016 feet below the runway), not the offset number.

PHAK 11-17 says a 10 percent excess landing speed causes at least a 21 percent increase in landing distance, and later on the same page that it causes 20 percent [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. Teach "about 20 percent or more".

AFH 9-28 says a learner should normally keep the first field until the instructor ends the exercise, while AFH 18-4 says not to hesitate to switch to an obviously better field, but only once [[24:199|AFH 9-28]] [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]. Both fit: switch only for a clearly better field within glide.

The AFH stabilized approach list includes a power setting not below the AFM minimum [[24:177|AFH 9-6]], which cannot apply with a failed engine. Teach the path, speed, configuration and sink rate elements.

Some troubleshooting items in this lesson (one magneto, boost pump, fixation) come from the AFH multiengine chapter [[24:283|AFH 13-34]]; they apply to any piston engine, but the POH restart list governs.
Application: teach touch and call for every shutdown item in simulated emergencies, and brief the go-around point and throttle control before each one [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].
Pair this lesson with Task CA.IX.A: the emergency descent is a separate maneuver with its own tolerances (ACS CA.IX.A).
Let students fly their chosen field until you end it so they see the result of their own errors, as the AFH suggests [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].
gaps: Best glide speed (and any weight-adjusted values), minimum sink speed, flap and gear advice, and the restart checklist are airplane-specific; use the POH/AFM.
The sources do not quantify how density altitude changes glide distance, and give no method to compute glide range in wind.
The ACS says to prepare for landing "as specified by the evaluator", but no source gives standard go-around heights for simulated forced landings; follow the examiner's brief and 14 CFR 91.119.
Altitude lost in a turn back is make-and-model specific; the AFH gives one example only and says to train it with an authorized instructor.
The AFH gives no hard rule for gear up or down at touchdown; it defers to the AFM/POH.

activities.title: Forced, precautionary or ditching?
activities.intro: Tap a situation, then tap the type of landing it is.

items.t: The engine seizes over farmland and will not restart
Weather closes in ahead and behind, so you land on a long hayfield with power
Oil pressure is slowly dropping, and you land at a private strip while the engine still runs
Lost and low on fuel, you choose a field and land with power
Fuel runs out on the way to a farm field and you glide the rest
The engine quits over a lake beyond gliding distance of the shore
With power, you set down on calm water because the shoreline is all trees

activities.title: Engine failure at night: the AFH list
activities.intro: Put the AFH night engine failure items in the order the AFH lists them, then tap Check.
steps: Keep control, set best glide, and turn toward an airport or away from congested areas
Check the fuel selector, magnetos and primer, and restart if you can
Announce the emergency to ATC or UNICOM
If the terrain is known and suitable, plan to land on an unlighted part of it
Complete the before-landing checklist and test the landing lights at altitude
Land in the normal landing attitude at the slowest possible airspeed
After landing, turn off all switches and get out quickly

activities.title: Reading a tree landing
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.

pins.label: Wing taking its share of the load in the branches
Windshield, protected because belly and wings hit first
Dense crowns close to the ground: the cushion
Heavy trunk: keep the fuselage off it
Gear torn away: dispensable structure used up

activities.title: True or false: configuration and touchdown
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Steep banks just before touchdown are fine as long as the airspeed is high.
cards.why: No. Steep banks near touchdown raise the stall speed and the risk of a wingtip strike [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

cards.s: In a tree landing you should steer between two trunks while still airborne so both wings take the load.
cards.why: No. Involve both wings between two trunks only once on the ground; do not try it while airborne [[24:355|AFH 18-6]].

cards.s: An airplane ditched at minimum speed in a normal attitude usually floats for at least several minutes.
cards.why: Yes. Intact wings and fuel tanks provide flotation for at least several minutes [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

cards.s: With little open space left in a confined area, forcing the airplane onto the ground can be better than waiting for it to settle.
cards.why: Yes. An airplane decelerates faster on the ground than in the air [[24:354|AFH 18-5]].

cards.s: Extend full flaps as soon as you pick a field, since they lower the stall speed.
cards.why: No. Flaps add drag and shorten the glide; premature flaps can ruin a sound plan [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

cards.s: Losing control of attitude and sink rate at touchdown is the most critical error in an emergency landing, even on ideal terrain.
cards.why: Yes. The AFH calls it the most critical and often the most inexcusable error [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

activities.title: Emergency radio and beacon tools
activities.intro: Tap an item, then tap what it does.

pairs.r: Distress: absolute priority and radio silence on the frequency
Urgency: priority over everything except distress
Squawk it when you cannot reach ATC right away
Guarded by DF stations, most civil towers and radar facilities
Detected by satellite and registered with NOAA
Set before a crash landing if fire risk is not a concern

activities.title: Forced landing numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Your airplane has an 11 to 1 glide ratio. In still air at best glide, about how far can you glide from 4,500 feet AGL, in nautical miles?
items.why: 11 to 1 means 11 feet forward for each foot down [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]: 4,500 x 11 = 49,500 feet. One NM is 6,076.1 feet [[1:398|PHAK 16-11]]: 49,500 / 6,076.1 = 8.1 NM.

items.q: You touch down at 50 knots airspeed with a 15-knot wind. How many times more destructive energy does a downwind touchdown carry than an into-wind one?
items.why: Groundspeeds are 50 + 15 = 65 knots and 50 - 15 = 35 knots. Energy goes with the square of groundspeed (double the speed, four times the energy) [[24:352|AFH 18-3]]: (65 / 35) squared = 1.857 squared = 3.4.

items.q: At a uniform 9 G, the AFH says a light airplane stops in about 9.4 feet from 50 mph. About how many feet does it need from 75 mph?
items.why: Stopping distance grows with the square of speed: 9.4 feet at 50 mph and 37.6 at 100 mph, four times as far [[24:352|AFH 18-3]]. 9.4 x (75 / 50) squared = 9.4 x 2.25 = 21.2 feet.

items.q: Your POH shows a 600-foot landing roll at sea level. Using about 3.5 percent per 1,000 feet, about how long is it at a 6,000-foot density altitude?
items.why: Landing distance grows about 3.5 percent per 1,000 feet [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]: 6 x 3.5 = 21 percent; 600 x 1.21 = 726 feet.

items.q: Using the AFH turn-back example values (4-second reaction, 3° per second, 1,000 fpm), how many degrees can you turn before reaching ground level after an engine failure at 700 feet AGL?
items.why: Time to the ground: 700 / 1,000 x 60 = 42 seconds. Minus 4 seconds reaction leaves 38 seconds; 38 x 3 = 114°, far short of the 225° the example needs [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

items.q: Gliding on final at 800 fpm after a complete power failure, about how many feet above the ground should you start slowing the descent?
items.why: Use a 10 percent lead, 100 feet at 1,000 fpm [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]: 10 percent of 800 = 80 feet.

activities.title: Engine failure on climbout
activities.intro: You are flying a fixed-gear four-seater out of a country airport, climbing at VY through 600 feet AGL. Wind is calm. Ahead is a road with poles along it, a wheat field slightly right, and woods to the left. The engine suddenly goes quiet.

steps.s: The engine has stopped. You are at VY, below best glide speed.
options: Lower the nose at once to best glide
Turn back to the runway right away
Hold the climb attitude while you troubleshoot
Pull up to gain a little height first
steps.why: At or below best glide, lower the nose immediately [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. In the initial climb, lower the nose and set the glide attitude [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

options: Straight onto the road
A slight right turn to the wheat field
The woods to the left
A 180° turn back to the runway
steps.why: Straight ahead or a slight turn is usually the lowest-risk choice [[24:356|AFH 18-7]]. Mature grain stops an airplane almost like an arresting device [[24:351|AFH 18-2]], while roads hide wires [[24:354|AFH 18-5]].

steps.s: You are lined up on the wheat field with a little time. What about the engine?
options: Spend your attention on a restart until it runs
A quick look at the fuel selector, mixture and magnetos only while you keep flying the glide
Ignore everything and turn off the master now
Pump the throttle until it catches
steps.why: Check the critical items that might restart the engine while planning the approach [[24:200|AFH 9-29]], but positive control comes first [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

steps.s: Near the ground, the field looks shorter than you hoped and a fence crosses the far end.
options: Pull up to stretch over the fence
Touch down slow and under control, accepting the fence at the end of the slide
Make a steep turn to find more room
Add flaps and hold it off until it stalls high
steps.why: Touch down at the lowest controllable speed [[24:352|AFH 18-3]]. Hitting an obstacle at the end of the ground slide is much less hazardous than hitting it at flying speed [[24:354|AFH 18-5]].

steps.s: You stop in the wheat, everyone unhurt. What now?
options: Leave the master on and wait inside
Turn off all switches, get everyone out, check the ELT is transmitting and stay with the airplane
Walk to the nearest town at once
Restart the engine to taxi out
steps.why: After landing, turn off all switches and get out [[24:230|AFH 11-13]]. Make sure the ELT works if needed [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]], and remain with the airplane unless you have good reason not to [[34:47|AIM 6-3-2]].
